t: Where the oracles against the nations sit
p: The Hebrew puts them last, in chapters 46-51. The Greek puts them in the middle, after 25:13, in another order.
b: In the Hebrew Bible the nations oracles close the book, just before the fall of Jerusalem retold in chapter 52. Their order is Egypt, Philistia, Moab, Ammon, Edom, Damascus, Kedar and Hazor, Elam, then Babylon (50-51). In the Greek (Septuagint) they follow 25:13 and run Elam, Egypt, Babylon, the Philistines, Edom, Ammon, Kedar, Damascus, Moab, as printed in Swete's edition. The same nations (with some others) drink the cup of wrath in 25:15-29, which the Greek moves next to them. Isaiah 13-23, Ezekiel 25-32 and Amos 1-2 have similar collections. Many commentators think they were spoken to Judah, not to the nations named.

p: Nebuchadnezzar beat the Egyptian army here, and Egypt's hopes in Syria ended.
b: Carchemish was a fortress city on the Euphrates. After Josiah died at Megiddo trying to stop Neco (2 Kings 23:29), Egypt held much of Syria. The Babylonian Chronicle (BM 21946) says that in Nabopolassar's twenty-first year his son Nebuchadnezzar crossed the river, defeated the Egyptian army at Carchemish and caught the survivors at Hamath, so that few returned home. Jeremiah's date, the fourth year of Jehoiakim, is the same year (compare Jeremiah 25:1; 36:1; 45:1). Afterward, as Kings puts it: "Egypt's king never again marched out of his land. The king of Babylon had seized everything from the Wadi of Egypt to the Euphrates River, all that used to belong to Egypt's king." (2 Kings 24:7)
r: 2 Kings 23:29; 2 Kings 24:7; 2 Chronicles 35:20; Jeremiah 25:1; Jeremiah 36:1; Jeremiah 45:1

p: Pharaoh from 610 to 595 BC. He killed Josiah, made Jehoiakim king, and lost Syria to Babylon.
b: Neco II (Egyptian Nekau, ruled 610-595 BC) marched north in 609 to help the last Assyrian forces. Josiah met him at Megiddo and was killed (2 Kings 23:29). Neco then put Jehoiakim on the throne of Judah in place of Jehoahaz (2 Kings 23:33-34). Herodotus says Neco also began a canal toward the Red Sea and sent Phoenician sailors around Africa (Histories 2.158-159, 4.42); he is reported by Herodotus, not by any text in the Bible.

p: The Hebrew siryon is armor made of small overlapping plates.
b: Siryon (also spelled shiryon, Jeremiah 51:3) is a coat of mail made of small metal scales sewn on a backing. The word is the same one used of Goliath's armor in 1 Samuel 17:5. The call in 46:3-4 sounds like a general's orders. Many readers hear it as mockery: Egypt drills for a battle that verse 5 shows already lost.

p: A cry Jeremiah uses again and again: 'terror from every side.'
b: The Hebrew magor missaviv is one of Jeremiah's trademarks (6:25; 20:10; 49:29; Lamentations 2:22). In 20:3 the priest Pashhur is renamed Magor-missabib after he beats the prophet. The phrase is also in Psalm 31:13. Here it is part of the picture of a rout: the Egyptians run and look in every direction and see only terror. See 20:3 for its first and best-known use in the book.
r: Jeremiah 6:25; Jeremiah 20:3; Jeremiah 20:10; Jeremiah 49:29; Psalm 31:13; Lamentations 2:22

p: Verses 3-4 are orders to an army; verse 5 shows it already broken. Is the first part a taunt?
b: The poem opens with orders (3-4), then the prophet says 'Why do I see it?' and describes the rout (5-6). Some commentators read 3-4 as ironic: the call to arms is Jeremiah's mock-heroic picture of Egypt marching out, and what he really sees is defeat. Others read the whole poem as a vision of the battle itself. Either way the verbs of 5-6 are in the perfect tense, as if the defeat has already happened, which is normal in prophecy that describes the future as done.

p: Egypt's yearly flood is the picture. The prophet turns Egypt's boast of rising into a boast that fails.
b: The Hebrew is ye'or, from the Egyptian word for the river (itrw), and 'rivers' are the Nile's channels in the Delta. The Nile rose each summer and covered the fields; the whole economy rested on it. Egypt says, in effect, 'I will rise and cover the land' (46:8). In 47:2 the picture turns around: waters rise from the north and flood the Philistine coast. Compare Ezekiel 29:3 and Amos 8:8.

p: Egypt's foreign troops: Nubians, Libyans (or Puntites) and men of Lud.
b: Cush is Nubia, south of Egypt. Put is usually Libya, west of Egypt; the Greek here has 'Libyans'. Lud (the 'Ludites') is debated: Lydia in Anatolia, whose soldiers may have served Egypt in the 600s, or an African people (Genesis 10:13 lists Ludim among Egypt's sons). The Greek has 'Lydians'. Egypt's armies were a mix of native troops and hired men, which prepares for 'her hired soldiers' in 46:21.
r: Genesis 10:6; Genesis 10:13; Ezekiel 27:10; Ezekiel 30:5; Nahum 3:9; Isaiah 66:19

p: A solemn title: Adonai YHWH tseva'ot.
b: Adonai YHWH tseva'ot joins 'Lord' (Adonai), the name YHWH (shown as GOD in capitals after 'Lord') and 'of Armies' (tseva'ot). 'Armies' may mean Israel's armies (1 Samuel 17:45), the angels, or the stars, or all of these. It is the title of the divine warrior, which fits a poem about a battle the LORD himself is fighting. Jeremiah uses it often in the nations oracles (46:25; 48:1; 49:5, 7, 26, 35).

p: The slaughter on the Euphrates is the LORD's feast, a sacrifice (zevach) with the sword as the priest's knife.
b: A zevach is a sacrificial meal. Calling a slaughter a sacrifice appears also in Isaiah 34:6 (at Bozrah), Zephaniah 1:7 and Ezekiel 39:17-20. The 'day' of this verse is a day of the LORD: not the end of the world but a time when he steps into history to settle accounts, here with Egypt's army (compare 'that day' in 30:7).

p: Balm came from Gilead. Egypt, famous for doctors, will find no cure.
b: Tsori, 'balm', was a resin traded from Gilead east of the Jordan (Genesis 37:25). Jeremiah asks in 8:22, 'Is there no balm in Gilead?' about Judah and uses the same picture here and in 51:8 about Babylon. Egypt had a long name for medicine: Herodotus says Egyptian doctors each treated one part of the body (Histories 2.84). The wound here cannot be treated.

p: A nation or city can be a 'daughter'; 'virgin' means not yet conquered.
b: Hebrew calls a people's capital or land 'the daughter of' the nation (Daughter Zion, Daughter Babylon). Betulah, 'virgin', here means a young woman who has never been taken: Egypt, which had never been conquered by a power from Mesopotamia in Jeremiah's day, is about to lose that status. Israel is also called 'virgin' in 31:4, 21 and Babylon in Isaiah 47:1.

a: when Nebuchadnezzar king of Babylon would come
p: A broken Babylonian tablet says Nebuchadnezzar went to fight Egypt in his thirty-seventh year. It does not say he conquered it.
b: The tablet BM 33041 (translated in Pritchard's ANET, p. 308) is badly broken. It says that in his thirty-seventh year (568/567 BC) Nebuchadnezzar marched against Egypt to fight, and it names Amasis as Egypt's king; the lines that would say what happened are lost. The break leaves open whether he entered Egypt itself or fought on its border. No Babylonian or Egyptian text that survives reports a conquest, and Amasis ruled until 526 BC. Jeremiah 43:8-13 and Ezekiel 29:17-20 also speak of Nebuchadnezzar and Egypt, so readers connect the tablet with them, but the tablet says only that a clash was planned or fought.

p: Egypt's north-eastern frontier town, its old capital, and a fort on the Delta road.
b: Migdol ('tower') was a frontier fortress in the north-east Delta, probably Tell el-Kedwa near Egypt's border with Sinai; Memphis (Hebrew Noph) was the old capital, near modern Cairo; Tahpanhes (Greek Daphnae, Tell Defenneh) was a fort on the road in. Jeremiah 44:1 lists Migdol, Tahpanhes and Memphis as places where Judean refugees lived, so some scholars think 46:13-26 was said to them (see the settings card). The Greek here has Magdolos and Memphis but no Tahpanhes.

a: Why was your mighty one thrown down?
t: The mighty one: Apis the bull?
p: The Hebrew word for 'mighty one' can also mean 'bull'. The Greek reads the Egyptian bull-god Apis.
b: The Hebrew 'abbir means 'strong one' and can mean 'bull' (Psalm 22:12 has the 'bulls' of Bashan). Here it is plural, 'abbirekha, with a singular verb ('was thrown down'), so it may be a plural of majesty for one mighty being, or the Greek may have heard the name of Apis, the sacred bull of Memphis (46:14), in it. The Greek reads 'Why did Apis flee from you? Your chosen bull did not stay', and the NRSV follows the Greek here. The Plain keeps the Hebrew and the singular; the Apis reading is in the variants. Verse 20, with its heifer, takes up the same cattle picture.

t: The oath, and who the King is
p: God swears by his own life. The King is the LORD, not Pharaoh.
b: 'As I live' (chai ani) is God's oath formula (Numbers 14:21; Ezekiel 5:11). The oath is followed by a title: 'the King ... whose name is the LORD of Armies', also used at 48:15 and 51:57. The title sets the real King against Pharaoh, whom the Egyptians call a god-king and whom the nations call 'all noise' (46:17). The invader 'like Tabor and Carmel' is not named; verses 13 and 26 say he is Nebuchadnezzar.

p: Egypt as a fine cow; the invader as a biting fly. The Hebrew word for the fly is rare.
b: Qerets appears only here in the Bible. 'Gadfly' or 'stinging fly' is the traditional guess; the Greek has apospasma, 'something torn off', and some read qerets as 'destruction'. Egypt as a cow fits its religion (the cow-goddess Hathor, and the Apis bull of Memphis, see 46:15), and a fly maddening a heifer is a good picture of an army driving a rich land into panic. Isaiah 7:18 also calls the Egyptians a fly, but 'from the Nile's streams'.

p: Egypt's pharaohs paid Greeks, Carians and others to fight. Judean soldiers served at Elephantine.
b: Herodotus says Pharaoh Psamtik I settled Ionian and Carian soldiers in Egypt (Histories 2.152, 2.154). Greek soldiers of Psamtik II scratched their names on the colossi at Abu Simbel about 591 BC, and Greek mercenaries fought for Apries and Amasis. Judean soldiers manned the border fortress at Elephantine (Aswan) by the 400s BC at the latest. The prophet says that those hired men, fat like calves in a stall, will be the first to bolt.

a: Her sound is like a snake creeping away
p: A hiss as Egypt slips off, or the sound of the invaders coming? The Hebrew leaves it open.
b: The line can mean that Egypt's voice dwindles like a hiss as the snake slides away, afraid. Some commentators add the picture of the rearing cobra (the uraeus) worn on Pharaoh's brow, which would make it a mock-royal image: the royal snake slinks off. Others think the 'voice' is the sound of the invaders' approach. The next line, 'for they march in with an army', supports the first reading.

p: Thebes (Hebrew No) was the home of Amun, king of the Egyptian gods.
b: 'No' is the Hebrew form of the Egyptian niwt, 'the city', the name of Thebes in Upper Egypt; Amun was its great god. Assyria sacked Thebes in 664/663 BC (Nahum 3:8-10 calls it No-Amon). Here the punishment reaches the gods (Amon, Pharaoh's divine patron), the king and all who trust in him. The Greek is much shorter (see the variant). Compare Ezekiel 30:14-16 and Jeremiah 43:12-13.

p: Like Moab, Ammon and Elam, Egypt gets a promise of return.
b: Four nations get a promise of restoration in these chapters: Egypt here, Moab (48:47), Ammon (49:6) and Elam (49:39). Edom, Damascus, Kedar and Hazor, and Philistia get none, and Babylon gets none. Ezekiel 29:13-16 promises that Egypt will be gathered after forty years but be a lowly kingdom; Isaiah 19:19-25 goes further and calls Egypt 'my people'. The Greek does not have this verse.

a: As for you, Jacob my servant
p: These two verses are nearly word for word 30:10-11 in the Book of Consolation.
b: 46:27-28 repeats 30:10-11. The Plain gives the shared Hebrew the same English as 30:10-11 and differs only where the Hebrew does: 46:27 lacks the words 'the LORD declares' that 30:10 has; 46:28 lacks 'to save you' (30:11 has it), puts 'the LORD declares' in the first line instead of after 'to save you', and has 'driven' where 30:11 has 'scattered'. Commentators disagree which came first. Some think a comfort poem for Israel was placed here as a counterweight to the doom on Egypt; others that the Book of Consolation took it from here. In both places Jacob is told that the nations will be finished but Israel will be disciplined, not ended. The Greek has these lines here (Greek 26:27-28) but leaves out 30:10-11 (Swete's Greek 37:10-11 is empty), which suggests the Greek's earlier edition had them only here.

a: I will not simply let you off
p: The same words God spoke on Sinai: he does not simply clear the guilty.
b: 'Will by no means clear the guilty' is part of the LORD's self-description in Exodus 34:7 (and Numbers 14:18, Nahum 1:3). Jeremiah turns it on Israel: the same God who is with them will not pretend their sins did not happen. 'Fairly' (lamishpat, literally 'by justice') means in proper measure: a limited punishment, in contrast to the 'full end' of the nations. Compare 10:24.

p: The heading gives a date nobody can fix for sure.
b: Several events have been proposed: Pharaoh Neco's capture of a city Herodotus calls Kadytis (often taken to be Gaza) after Megiddo, about 609 BC (Histories 2.159); a campaign by Psamtik I; Apries's attack on the coast about 588; and Psamtik II. The Babylonian Chronicle adds that Nebuchadnezzar took Ashkelon in the month of Kislev 604 BC, imprisoned its king and turned the city into ruins, and excavations at Ashkelon found the burned layer (Stager). The Greek heading lacks the clause about Pharaoh and Gaza. This poem fits the Babylonian blow at Ashkelon (47:5-7), though no text says so.

a: waters are coming up from the north
p: The same enemy as in 'the foe from the north', pictured as a flood.
b: Jeremiah's northern foe (1:14-15; 4:6; 6:1, 22; 25:9) is here a flash flood rolling down a dry streambed (nachal). Isaiah 8:7-8 pictures Assyria as the Euphrates in flood; 46:7-8 pictured Egypt as the Nile. Here the pictures run into each other: Egypt rose like the Nile, but a bigger flood comes from the north and sweeps the coast. The 'city' in the singular may be Gaza or Ashkelon.

p: The Philistines' homeland in the Bible, probably Crete or a nearby Aegean land.
b: Amos 9:7 says the LORD brought the Philistines from Caphtor, and Deuteronomy 2:23 says Caphtorites drove out the earlier people of Gaza's region. Caphtor is usually identified with Crete, or the wider Aegean (Egyptian Keftiu). The Hebrew has the singular 'i, 'island', which can also mean 'coast'. 2QJer and the Greek have 'islands' (see the variant). Archaeology confirms Aegean-style pottery in Philistine towns after about 1175 BC.

p: Gashing the skin and shaving the head were mourning rites, forbidden to Israel.
b: Mourners in many ancient lands cut themselves and shaved their heads. Israel's law forbids it (Leviticus 19:28; Deuteronomy 14:1), yet Jeremiah mentions it of Israelites (16:6; 41:5) and of Moab (48:37). The Hebrew verb here is titgodedi; 2QJer and the Greek read it differently (see the variants). Baldness at Gaza and silence at Ashkelon are a picture of two cities in mourning.

p: Who is crying, 'How long?' And why can the sword not rest?
b: Hoy, 'Alas', is the call of a funeral lament. The speaker is not named. Many take it as Jeremiah's own plea, like 'How long?' in the laments (4:21; 12:4). Others hear the Philistine survivors begging the sword to stop. The answer in 47:7 is stern: the sword has orders. The picture of the LORD's sword (Deuteronomy 32:41-42; Isaiah 34:5-6; Ezekiel 21:3-5) makes the war God's own act. The Greek says 'how long will you cut, sword of the Lord?' and joins the earlier question to it.

p: Moab lay on the plateau east of the Dead Sea. This is the longest of the nations oracles and borrows most.
b: Moab was Israel's neighbor and relative (Genesis 19:37), home of Ruth, and often an enemy (Numbers 22-25; 2 Kings 3). King Mesha's stele, found in 1868 at Dibon, names many of the towns in this chapter. Jeremiah 48 reuses Isaiah 15-16 (see the table on the chapter page), Numbers 21:28-29 and 24:17, and Isaiah 24:17-18. In 594/593 BC envoys from Moab and its neighbors came to Zedekiah in Jerusalem (27:3; the Hebrew of 27:1 says Jehoiakim, which many read as a slip for Zedekiah, as 27:3 and 27:12 suggest). Moab had earlier sent raiders against Judah (2 Kings 24:2). Josephus says Nebuchadnezzar subdued Ammon and Moab in his twenty-third year, 582 BC.

t: Nebo, Kiriathaim and the high fort
p: Nebo here is a town, not the famous mountain. Mesha's stele names both Nebo and Kiriathaim.
b: This Nebo is a town near Mount Nebo (Numbers 32:3, 38), where Moses saw the land (Deuteronomy 34:1). On the Mesha Stele, Chemosh tells Mesha to take Nebo from Israel, and Mesha says he rebuilt Kiriathaim. 'The high fort' is misgab (the Greek takes it as two place names); it can also be a general word for a fortress or a place name.

a: In Heshbon they have planned evil
p: A pun: Heshbon (cheshbon) and 'planned' (chashevu).
b: Be-Cheshbon chashevu: 'in Heshbon they planned.' The wordplay cannot be kept in English. Heshbon was the city of the Amorite king Sihon (Numbers 21:26) and was later claimed by Reuben, Gad and Moab in turn. Here Moab's own Heshbon is where its enemies plot, and in 49:3 Heshbon is told to howl along with Ammon's Rabbah, so the frontier moved with the powers.

p: The name looks like English 'mad men' but is a Moabite town; there is a pun on 'be silent'.
b: Madmen (Hebrew madmen) is an unidentified town of Moab; do not read it as 'madmen'. The verb 'will be struck dumb' (tidommi) from damam, 'be silent', sounds like it. Some link it with the Dimon of Isaiah 15:9. The Greek has no Madmen here.

a: Chemosh will go out into exile
p: In the ancient world a conquered people's statues, priests and officials were taken away. Chemosh was Moab's national god.
b: Chemosh appears in Numbers 21:29, Judges 11:24, 1 Kings 11:7, 33 and 2 Kings 23:13. On the Mesha Stele he is angry with his land, then gives Mesha victory and orders him to take Nebo. Ancient conquerors did carry off the images of conquered gods (Isaiah 46:1-2; 1 Samuel 5:1-2). The same threat is made against Ammon's Milcom in 49:3. To Israel's prophets this shows that such gods cannot protect their own people. 2 Kings 3:27 reports that Mesha sacrificed his firstborn son on the wall; whether that was to Chemosh is not stated.
r: Numbers 21:29; Judges 11:24; 1 Kings 11:7; 2 Kings 3:27; 2 Kings 23:13; Isaiah 46:1-2

p: The Hebrew word tsits is rare. See the variant for the three main readings.
b: Tsits usually means 'blossom' (Isaiah 28:1) or the gold plate on the high priest's turban (Exodus 28:36). 'Wings' is not what the word means; it is a guess from the next words, 'she will surely fly off', and the Plain follows it for lack of a better fit. The Vulgate has 'flower', and the Greek 'signs' (probably tsiyyun, 'marker'). Some English versions have 'salt', picturing a ruin sown with salt (compare Judges 9:45); that is also a guess from the context.

a: Cursed is the one who does the LORD's work in a lazy way
p: The curse is aimed at the invader who must carry out the LORD's judgment. It has been quoted for violence.
b: 'The LORD's work' is the war he gives Babylon to do; holding back the sword would be disobedience, as when Saul spared Agag (1 Samuel 15:9-23) or when Ahab spared Ben-hadad (1 Kings 20:42). Radak, as reported in Sefaria's Hebrew text, applies the curse to any warrior in the war who lets his hand slack. Readers have quoted it to excuse cruelty; the verse itself is about a judgment on Moab by an army, not a rule for believers. See Holy war.

p: Wine kept on the sediment keeps its strong taste but is never made clear. Moab never had to change.
b: Winemakers poured wine off from jar to jar to separate it from the sediment (the dregs, Hebrew shemarim). Wine left too long on the dregs stayed thick and sweet. The picture: Moab has had calm for generations, no exile and no shaking, so its pride and its habits have stayed as they were. Zephaniah 1:12 uses the same image of Judah's complacent men; Psalm 75:8 uses 'dregs' of the cup of wrath. In 48:12 the pourers arrive.

t: Moab ashamed of Chemosh, Israel of Bethel
p: Bethel's golden calf was the northern kingdom's place of trust, and it failed them.
b: Jeroboam I put a golden calf at Bethel (1 Kings 12:28-29). Hosea 10:5-6 says the people of Samaria would mourn it and that it would be carried to Assyria, a source of shame. Jeremiah's point is plain: Moab's god will let Moab down as Bethel's calf let Israel down. Israel's northern kingdom fell in 722 BC, an example the Judean hearers knew well.

p: Moab's ruler and power, pictured as a king's scepter.
b: A staff (matteh) or rod (maqqel) can be a shepherd's tool or a king's scepter. Numbers 24:17 said a scepter would rise from Israel and smash the brows of Moab; Jeremiah says Moab's own scepter is broken. The neighbors are told to feel for it, perhaps with a note of irony, since the same neighbors share its fate.

p: Dibon (modern Dhiban) was Mesha's capital, where his stele was set up.
b: Mesha says on his stone that he built Dibon and its highway at the Arnon. Isaiah 15:2 has the same town, where its people go up to wail. Here 'Daughter Dibon' is told to step down from honor, meaning her pride and place as capital.

p: Aroer stood on the rim of the Arnon gorge beside the main road.
b: Aroer was on the northern edge of the Arnon gorge (Deuteronomy 2:36; Joshua 13:9), above the road later called the King's Highway (Numbers 20:17; 21:22). The Mesha Stele says Mesha built Aroer and made the highway at the Arnon. The people of Aroer are told to stand by the road and question runaways, which means the news from the north will reach them first.

p: A list of towns on the plateau that once belonged to Reuben.
b: The plateau (mishor) north of the Arnon was given to Reuben (Joshua 13:15-23). Over the centuries Moab took it back, and the Mesha Stele names Nebo, Dibon, Kiriathaim, Beth-diblathaim, Beth-meon (Baal-meon) and Jahaz as places Mesha built or took. Jeremiah's list is a map of the whole region from the Arnon north to Heshbon. The lists in Joshua 13 and Jeremiah 48 overlap in many names.

p: Not the Edomite Bozrah of 49:13, 22. Often identified with Bezer.
b: Edom's Bozrah (Buseirah) appears in 49:13 and 49:22. The Bozrah of Moab is a different place on the plateau, often identified with Bezer, a town Mesha says he built. Place names repeat across the region: there is more than one Bozrah, and more than one Aroer.

p: Horn means strength, arm means power.
b: The horn of a bull, lifted high, was a picture of strength (1 Samuel 2:10; Psalm 75:10). The arm is the striking power of a warrior or a king (Ezekiel 30:21, where Pharaoh's arm is broken). Together they say that Moab has lost both its pride and its strength to fight.

t: The cup of the LORD's anger
p: Drunkenness is a picture of judgment: the nation staggers and is sick.
b: In 25:15-29 the LORD gives Jeremiah a cup of the wine of his anger to make the nations drink; Moab is on the list (25:21). Here the command is to 'make him drunk', and the result is vomit and shame. Habakkuk 2:15-16, Isaiah 51:17-23 and Lamentations 4:21 use the same image, and Revelation 14:10 takes it up. In 49:12 Edom is told it too must drink.
r: Jeremiah 25:15-29; Jeremiah 49:12; Jeremiah 51:7; Isaiah 51:17-23; Habakkuk 2:15-16; Revelation 14:10

a: Was Israel not a laughingstock to you?
p: Moab's boasting over Israel is recorded on Mesha's own stone: 'Israel has perished forever.'
b: Mesha's stele says Omri's house oppressed Moab, and then that 'Israel has perished forever.' When Judah fell, Moab's neighbors rejoiced (Ezekiel 25:8; Lamentations 2:15-16; Zephaniah 2:8-10 speaks of Moab's taunts). The Plain uses 'laughingstock' for this word (sechoq) in 48:26, 27 and 39, so the reader can see the turn: Moab laughed at Israel and will be laughed at. Jeremiah's question is bitter: Israel was not caught among thieves; why was Moab shaking its head? The same verb (nud) in 48:17 is the neighbors' sympathy, so it can mean either.

a: We have heard of Moab's pride
p: Isaiah 16:6 says almost the same. Pride is the sin named again and again against Moab.
b: Pride (ga'on) is the sin charged against Moab in Isaiah 16:6, Isaiah 25:10-11, Zephaniah 2:10 and here and in 48:26, 42. Jeremiah 48:29 uses four words for pride, which the Plain keeps apart: gaon (pride), gavhoo (loftiness), ga'avah (proudness) and rum lev (height of heart). It is not the pride of a bad temper but of security: the nation 'sat on its dregs' (48:11) and trusted its works (48:7).

p: The Hebrew says simply 'not so' (lo ken): the boast is not right.
b: Lo ken, 'not so', is also in Isaiah 16:6 (the same line). It means that what Moab says and does is not true, not honest. 'Rings false' keeps the sense in English. 2QJer has this verse in part. It reads 'she did' where the Masoretic Text has 'they did' (the last word), and otherwise differs only in spelling.

a: That is why I howl for Moab
p: Jeremiah, the LORD, or a poet's persona weeping over an enemy?
b: Verses 31-36 say 'I howl', 'I cry', 'my heart throbs'. Isaiah 16:9-11 has the same. The speaker could be the prophet (as in 4:19; 9:1), the LORD who also says 'I have stopped the wine' (48:33), or a conventional mourner. Rabbinic tradition praised this: Israel's prophets wept for the nations while Balaam tried to curse a whole people (Numbers Rabbah 20:1, as the Isaiah 15 page cites). Brian Jones argues the Isaiah version is ironic mourning. This site adds a thought of its own, not Jones's: the promise of restoration 'in the last days' (48:47), which Isaiah lacks, may count against reading Jeremiah's version as mockery.

p: Karmel here means orchard or garden country, not the mountain.
b: Hebrew karmel means a planted, fruitful land. Mikkarmel is 'from the garden land' (Isaiah 16:10; compare Isaiah 29:17; 32:15). The harvest shout (heidad) was the cheer of the grape treaders; when it fails, joy has gone. 2QJer preserves 'from the land of Moab' here and agrees with the Masoretic Text. The verb in 'I have stopped the wine' (hishbati) is the one Isaiah 16:10 uses of the harvest shout, where the Plain has 'silenced'; here its object is the wine, so the Plain says 'stopped'.

p: Mesha says he made a high place for Chemosh.
b: The Mesha Stele says he built 'this high place for Chemosh' at Qarhoh (a name that may or may not be the Kir-heres of verse 31). Moab's high places are also in Isaiah 16:12; Solomon built one for Chemosh (1 Kings 11:7) and Josiah destroyed it (2 Kings 23:13). Only Chemosh is named on the stele; the plural 'gods' here is the usual Hebrew way of speaking of foreign worship.

p: Flutes were played at funerals. Jeremiah's heart plays the funeral tune.
b: Hebrew chalil is a reed pipe. The Mishnah says even the poorest family in Israel must hire at least two flutes and one wailing woman for a funeral (Ketubot 4:4), and Matthew 9:23 shows flute players at a house of death. Isaiah 16:11 has 'a harp' where Jeremiah has 'flutes'. The Greek says the heart 'drones' (bombesousin), a sound like a pipe.

a: like a jar no one wants
p: Jeremiah uses this image of a nation or king broken like pottery.
b: 'A vessel in which there is no pleasure' occurs for Moab here, for Coniah in 22:28 and for Israel in Hosea 8:8. It belongs with the potter's images (18:1-11) and the shattered jar of 19:10-11. A broken jar is not mended; it is thrown out. Egyptian execration texts of the Middle Kingdom wrote enemy rulers' names on pots and then smashed them, a similar idea.

a: like an eagle he swoops down
p: The eagle stands for the invader. The same lines are at 49:22.
b: The eagle is Nebuchadnezzar in Ezekiel 17:3 and the Babylonian horsemen in Habakkuk 1:8. Here the Hebrew has 'he' without a name. The same two verses are used for Edom's Bozrah in 49:22. The Greek of 48:40-41 lacks the eagle and the 'woman in labor' line, and reads 'Ekron' for 'Kerioth' (see the variant).

p: Three sound-alike words: terror, pit, snare.
b: In Hebrew the three words rhyme: pachad, pachat, pach. Isaiah 24:17-18 has the same triple (see that passage; many critical scholars date Isaiah 24-27 late, in which case Jeremiah's use would be the earlier, but the direction of borrowing is debated), and Amos 5:19 has a similar chain of escapes that end badly. The line is a trap-within-a-trap: run from one danger and you find the next.

a: a flame from the midst of Sihon
p: Jeremiah turns the Israelites' victory song over Sihon (Numbers 21:28-29) into a song of doom for Moab.
b: Numbers 21:28 says: "For fire went out from Heshbon, / a flame from the town of Sihon." Numbers 21:29: "Woe to you, Moab! / You are lost, people of Chemosh!" Jeremiah 48:45-46 uses both: the fire now comes from Heshbon against Moab, the old capital of the Amorite king. 'Sons of noise' (bene sha'on) echoes Numbers 24:17 where some read 'sons of Sheth'. The old song celebrated Sihon's conquest of Moab; here it is turned back. The Greek lacks verses 45-47; 2QJer preserves most of verse 45 as far as 'and a flame' (see the variants).

p: A promise to restore. The phrase puns on shuv, 'turn', Jeremiah's key word.
b: Shav shevut (here shavti shevut) is literally 'turn the turning' or, as the KJV has it, 'bring back the captivity'. It is a stock phrase for restoring fortunes: Job's in Job 42:10, Israel's in 30:3, 18; 31:23; 32:44; 33:7, 11, 26. It also contains the verb shuv, 'turn back', which Jeremiah plays on everywhere. Here it is a promise to Moab, 'in the last days', that Moab will not be wiped out forever. See 49:6, 39.

p: Ammon's capital Rabbah is modern Amman. Its king Baalis plotted against Gedaliah.
b: Ammon lay east of the Jordan around Rabbah (modern Amman). Its god was Milcom (see below). In 40:14 and 41:10, 15 Baalis king of the Ammonites sent Ishmael to murder Gedaliah. In 1984 a clay seal impression was found at Tell el-'Umeiri in Jordan that reads 'belonging to Milkom-or, servant of Baalis', from about 600 BC (Herr). Amos 1:13-15 has an earlier oracle against Ammon and Rabbah; 49:2-3 echoes it.

p: Ammon moved into Gad's old territory after Assyria emptied it.
b: Gad's land lay east of the Jordan (Joshua 13:24-28). Tiglath-pileser III carried off the people of Gilead about 734-732 BC (2 Kings 15:29; 1 Chronicles 5:26), and Ammon occupied the empty land. The question 'Does Israel have no heirs?' uses the language of inheritance: the verb is yarash, 'inherit' or 'dispossess' (see 49:2).

p: The same letters mean 'their king' (malkam) and the name of Ammon's god.
b: The Hebrew mlkm is vowelled malkam, 'their king', in 49:1, 3, but is the same word as the Milcom of 1 Kings 11:5, 33 and 2 Kings 23:13. The Greek has Melchol (Milcom). Amos 1:15 has the same word with 'he and his officials'. Context favors the god, since 49:3 gives him 'priests', and so does the parallel with Chemosh (48:7). Milcom is not the same as Molech (see that topic), though the names come from the same root, 'king'.

a: Then Israel will take over from those who took over from him
p: A wordplay: yarash means both 'inherit' and 'dispossess'.
b: Veyarash Yisra'el et yorashav: 'Israel will inherit from his inheritors.' The same verb ran through verse 1 ('heir', 'has taken over'). The verse promises that the ones who took Gad's land will be dispossessed in turn. It does not say how or when; Ammon's land was not given to Israel in later history.

p: Rabbah is modern Amman. David took it (2 Samuel 11-12); Amos threatened it with fire.
b: Rabbah, 'the big one', held a famous iron bed said to belong to Og (Deuteronomy 3:11). Joab besieged it for David (2 Samuel 11:1; 12:26-31). Amos 1:14 says: fire in the wall of Rabbah, shouts on the day of battle. Jeremiah borrows 'a shout of battle' (teru'ah) and the fire. 'Daughter towns' are the villages around a city.

p: Not the Ai of Joshua. An Ammonite town of that name is unknown.
b: The Ai of Joshua 7-8 was west of the Jordan near Bethel, so this must be another place (or a changed text). The Greek does not have 'Ai'. It may be an Ammonite town otherwise unknown. Heshbon is called to howl, though in chapter 48 it is Moab's: see 48:2.

p: The Hebrew gederot are the walls or hedges around a sheepfold.
b: Gederah is the stone wall of a sheepfold or of a farm enclosure (Numbers 32:16, 24; Psalm 89:40). The KJV has 'hedges'. People run back and forth along the walls because there are no real fortifications in the countryside: they have no safe place. Some think a place called 'Gederoth' is meant.

p: Shovavah is Jeremiah's word for faithless Israel; here it is used of Ammon.
b: Shovav and shovavah come from shuv, 'turn'. Jeremiah calls Israel the 'turning-away' one (3:14, 22; 31:22). Applying the same word to Ammon is bitter irony: Ammon's land is held by one who has turned away. The 'valley that flows' (zav) may be a fruitful land or may flow away; the Greek has 'Anakim' for 'valleys' (see the variant).

p: Teman in Edom was known for wise men. Eliphaz, Job's friend, was a Temanite.
b: Teman was an Edomite region (Genesis 36:11, 15). Its wise men are remembered in Job 2:11 (Eliphaz the Temanite) and in Obadiah 8. Baruch 3:22-23, a book some churches count as Scripture, says the sons of Hagar and the merchants of Merran and Teman have not found the way of wisdom. The wisdom that fails in verses 7-10 is the cleverness of statecraft: it did not read the signs of Babylon's coming.

p: A trading oasis in north-west Arabia (al-Ula), tied to Edom by trade.
b: Dedan is named as a caravan station in Isaiah 21:13 and Ezekiel 27:15, 20. The Babylonian king Nabonidus campaigned in north Arabia about 553-543 BC, including Tayma and Dedan; he lived at Tayma for years. The Greek has Daidam. The people are told to 'go down deep to live', which means into caves or far into the desert.

a: If grape harvesters came to you
p: Jeremiah 49:9 is close to Obadiah 5, in a different order.
b: Grape pickers leave something for the poor (Leviticus 19:10; Deuteronomy 24:21). Even thieves leave something. But the LORD strips Esau clean. Obadiah 5 asks the same two questions in the opposite order (thieves first, then grape pickers), adds 'how you are destroyed!', and says the thieves 'steal' (yignevu) where Jeremiah says they 'wreck' (hishchitu). The Edom oracles of Jeremiah 49:7-22 and Obadiah 1-9 overlap in several places (see the table on the chapter page).

p: Esau is the ancestor of Edom, Jacob's twin. The poem uses his name for the nation.
b: Genesis 25-36 makes Esau (also called Edom) the ancestor of the Edomites. The prophets called Edom 'brother' of Israel (Obadiah 10, 12; Amos 1:11; Deuteronomy 23:7). 'Esau' is used for the nation in Obadiah 6, 8, 18 and in Malachi 1:2-5. The 'secret places' are hidden storage and hideouts in the Edomite rock country.

t: Mercy for the fatherless in Edom
p: A surprise in a doom oracle: the LORD cares for Edom's orphans and widows.
b: The LORD is known as the father of orphans and defender of widows (Psalm 68:5; Deuteronomy 10:18). Here this care reaches the families Edom's war leaves behind, an unexpected kindness. Readers differ: some hear a hint of mercy, others a sad irony. Hosea 14:3 says 'in you the orphan finds mercy.'

t: Who was not meant to drink?
p: The people 'not sentenced to drink' are probably Judah, whom God spares less than he spares Edom.
b: Many commentators take those who were not sentenced to drink as Judah, who drank first (25:18, 29). The logic is: if the people who belong to the LORD must drink, how can the unrelated Edom escape? 25:29 has the same sentence ('you will not go unpunished'). Another reading takes them as innocent people in Edom's war, such as the orphans and widows of 49:11. The cup is the cup of wrath (see 48:26).

a: I have sworn by my own self
p: God swore by himself to bless Abraham (Genesis 22:16). Here the oath is a curse.
b: In Genesis 22:16 (and Hebrews 6:13) the oath by God's own self secures a promise. In Jeremiah it also secures judgment (22:5; 51:14; Amos 6:8). Bozrah, probably Buseirah in Jordan, was Edom's chief city; Isaiah 34:6 and Amos 1:12 also name it. Excavations there found a large city of the 700s-600s BC (Bienkowski).
r: Genesis 22:16; Hebrews 6:13; Jeremiah 22:5; Jeremiah 51:14; Isaiah 34:6; Amos 1:12

a: I have heard a report from the LORD
p: These verses are almost the same as Obadiah 1-4. Which came first?
b: Jeremiah 49:14-16 matches Obadiah 1-4 (49:15 with Obadiah 2, 49:16 with Obadiah 3-4), and 49:9-10 matches Obadiah 5-6. Views: (1) Obadiah used Jeremiah (Obadiah 11-14 refers to Jerusalem's fall, so it is later than 586); (2) Jeremiah used Obadiah, which some date earlier; (3) both used an older oracle against Edom. Scholars are split, and no view is a consensus. Jewish tradition says Obadiah was a convert from Edom (Babylonian Talmud, Sanhedrin 39b). Obadiah will follow Jeremiah's wording where the Hebrew is the same.

p: The Hebrew word occurs only here. It may mean the terror Edom spreads, or an idol.
b: The word tiflatsteka (from palats, 'shudder') is found only here. It may mean 'the horror you cause'. A related word, mifletset, is used of a 'horrid thing', an image of Asherah, in 1 Kings 15:13, so some read 'your horrid idol'. The Greek has paignia, 'your play' or 'your jest'. The Plain keeps 'terror you cause' as the likeliest sense.

p: Edom's strongholds were cut into red sandstone cliffs; Petra later became the Nabatean capital.
b: Edom was a mountain land with cliffs and canyons. 'Sela' ('the rock') is a name for its stronghold (2 Kings 14:7; Isaiah 16:1). Umm el-Biyara above Petra has an Edomite settlement of the 600s BC. The Nabateans took the region over by the 300s BC, and the Edomites (Idumeans) moved into southern Judea. The family of Herod the Great was Idumean.

a: As when Sodom and Gomorrah were overturned
p: Used again for Babylon in 50:40.
b: 'Overturned' (mahpekhah) is the verb of Sodom's end (Genesis 19:25; Deuteronomy 29:23; Isaiah 13:19). Jeremiah 50:40 repeats the sentence against Babylon. The Hebrew differs in two small ways: 50:40 names God ('as when God overturned') and has 'the LORD declares' (ne'um) where 49:18 has 'the LORD says' (amar). The Plain gives both verses the same English, with 'declares' in both. In this oracle it falls on Edom, where Malachi 1:3-4 says the LORD made Esau's hill country a desolation.

p: Lions lived in the thickets along the Jordan until the Middle Ages.
b: The Jordan's banks were overgrown with willows and reeds, a hiding place for lions (Jeremiah 12:5; Zechariah 11:3). The lion here is the LORD, who drives the flock from its safe pasture. The same verses (19-20) are used against Babylon in 50:44-45. The Hebrew differs there only in 'him' (49:19) against 'them' (50:44) and in the names (Edom and Teman against Babylon and the Chaldeans); the Plain of 50:44-45 uses this wording except at those points. The 'chosen one' set over the pasture is understood as Nebuchadnezzar or another agent of the LORD, as in 27:6.

p: Probably the Gulf of Aqaba, Edom's own sea.
b: The Sea of Reeds is usually the Red Sea. Here it is likely the Gulf of Aqaba, which touched Edom's land (1 Kings 9:26). The cry of Edom's fall is heard at the southern limit of the country.

a: There is anxiety on the sea
t: On the sea or like the sea?
p: The Hebrew says 'in the sea'; many correct it to 'like the sea', as in Isaiah 57:20.
b: The Hebrew bayyam is 'in the sea'. Many commentators read kayyam, 'like the sea', which fits Isaiah 57:20 (the wicked are like the sea that cannot rest). The Greek leaves out the sea. Hamath and Arpad were Aramean city-states that fell to Assyria in 720 and 740 BC (Isaiah 10:9; 36:19), so the verse looks backward, or the oracle uses older material.

p: A royal name of Damascus, 'son of Hadad', used by several kings.
b: Ben-hadad ('son of the storm god Hadad') was the name of at least two or three kings of Aram-Damascus (1 Kings 15:18; 20:1; 2 Kings 13:3). Amos 1:4 says almost the same: fire on the house of Hazael that eats the citadels of Ben-hadad. Since Damascus fell to Assyria in 732 BC, many scholars think the oracle recycles old language.

p: This Hazor is an Arab settlement; Hebrew hatsor means enclosure or village.
b: The Hazor of Joshua 11 stands in the north of Israel. The 'Hazor' of 49:28-33 belongs to Arabs of the desert, 'the people of the East'. Hatsor means 'enclosure, settled camp' (compare Genesis 25:16, 'by their settlements'). The Greek calls it 'the queen of the court' (basilissa tes aules). The Babylonian Chronicle reports that in the sixth year of Nebuchadnezzar (599/598 BC) he sent his troops into the desert and took much plunder from the Arabs.

p: A large Arab tribal group, descended from Ishmael's son Kedar.
b: Kedar was a son of Ishmael (Genesis 25:13). Isaiah 21:16-17 says Kedar's glory would end within a year; Assyrian records name Kedarite kings and queens, and Ashurbanipal fought them. They were herders and caravan traders, known for black tents (Song of Songs 1:5).
r: Genesis 25:13; Isaiah 21:16-17; Song of Songs 1:5; Ezekiel 27:21

p: The 'sons of the East' are the desert peoples east of Judah.
b: Bene qedem are the peoples of the desert east of Israel: Midian and Amalek raiders (Judges 6:3), Job (Job 1:3). Ezekiel 25:4, 10 says Ammon will be given to them. The area is the Syrian-Arabian desert.

a: those who cut the hair at their temples
p: A mark of certain Arab tribes. Herodotus reports a similar practice.
b: Qetsutse pe'ah means those with the hair at the edge (pe'ah) of the head cut. The phrase also appears in 9:26 and 25:23, where it marks desert peoples. Herodotus says the Arabs cut their hair in a circle and shave around the temples (Histories 3.8). Israel's law forbade cutting the edges of the head and beard (Leviticus 19:27), which shows the practice marked foreign worship.

p: The same fate as Jerusalem (9:11) and Babylon (51:37).
b: The jackal, a scavenger, lives in ruins in the prophets (Isaiah 13:22; 34:13). Jeremiah says it will be the home of Jerusalem's ruins (9:11), Judah's cities (10:22), Hazor (here) and Babylon (51:37). The phrase 'no one will live there' is repeated from 49:18.

a: early in the reign of Zedekiah
p: Elam, in south-west Iran, is the farthest nation. The date is 597/596 BC.
b: Nebuchadnezzar made Zedekiah king in 597 BC (2 Kings 24:17). Elam, with its capital at Susa, had been broken by Ashurbanipal of Assyria about 646 BC; Ezra 4:9-10 mentions Elamites settled in Samaria by 'Osnappar'. By Jeremiah's day it was weak, and later Cyrus's Anshan lay in old Elamite lands. The Greek puts the Elam oracle first, at 25:14-19 (Swete's numbering), with the heading 'at the beginning of the reign of Zedekiah' at the start of the Egypt chapter.

p: Elam was known for its archers.
b: Isaiah 22:6 says 'Elam took up the quiver'. Elamite archers also appear in Assyrian reliefs and later in the Persian army. 'The bow' stands for Elam's military power. 'The first and best of their strength' translates reshit gevuratam, 'the beginning of their might'.

p: Winds from all four corners of the sky; a number of totality.
b: The four winds are the four directions, so Elam is scattered everywhere. The picture recurs in Daniel 7:2, Zechariah 2:6 and Revelation 7:1. 'No nation where Elam's outcasts do not go' foretells exile and spread. Acts 2:9 lists Elamites among the pilgrims at Pentecost: "We are Parthians, Medes and Elamites."

a: I will place my throne in Elam
p: The LORD sets up his judgment seat in a foreign land.
b: Nebuchadnezzar's throne is to be set at Tahpanhes in Egypt (43:10), and foreign kings set thrones at Jerusalem's gates in 1:15. Here the LORD himself presides at Elam, as a judge at a trial: he removes the king and officials. This is the only place in the oracles where God's throne is placed in a foreign land.

t: Elam, Pentecost and the last days
p: A promise to Elam, 'in the last days'. Acts 2:9 names Elamites at Pentecost.
b: The promise is the last of the four restorations (see 46:26). Christian readers have connected it with Acts 2:9: Elamites were among those who heard the apostles at Pentecost. Others see no connection and read a plain restoration of the people in the age to come. The Greek of 25:19 has the promise too (Swete's numbering).
